title: Korea
hookLine: a monk arrives in a Korean kingdom carrying images and texts, and the teaching takes root

cards: A monk arrives at a royal court on a peninsula, and he isn't traveling light. He brings images of the Buddha and written scriptures, a gift from a Chinese ruler to a Korean king. The king could send him back.
He could lock the gifts in a treasury and forget them. Or he could do something that would change his country's story for a very long time. Today the road leaves China and turns east, to Korea.

teach.b: Korea was then three kingdoms: Goguryeo in the north, Baekje in the southwest, Silla in the southeast.
The old Korean history called the Samguk Sagi records that in 372 a Chinese ruler sent the monk Sundo to Goguryeo with images and scriptures, and that King Sosurim received him.
Within a few years, the same history says, temples were built for monks to live in.

The welcome wasn't the same everywhere. Baekje, the history says, welcomed a foreign monk too, the teaching spread there, and from Baekje it would later travel on across the sea. Silla held out longer.
A Korean collection of stories called the Samguk Yusa tells of Ichadon, a young official at the Silla court. The king wanted to honor the Buddha's teaching; his nobles refused.
Ichadon offered to take the blame and be put to death. The story says that when he was executed, his blood ran white like milk, and the frightened court stopped resisting.
Whatever readers make of the milk, Korean Buddhist tradition remembers him as the one who opened the door in Silla. A teaching doesn't land like a parcel.
It comes in a monk's bag, gets a hearing at a court, meets suspicion, and slowly takes on the shape of the people who receive it.
In the days ahead, Korea will give it its own thinkers, its own debates, and one very large library.

how: Korean Buddhists remember Sundo's arrival in Goguryeo and Ichadon's death in Silla as founding moments, and Ichadon is still honored in Korea as a martyr who opened the way for the teaching.

games.q: you're Ichadon at the Silla court. the king wants to honor the Buddha's teaching, and the nobles refuse. what do you do?
o: offer to take the blame and be put to death.
slip away to China to study.
games.why: in the Samguk Yusa, Ichadon offers his life. his blood runs white like milk, and the court stops resisting.

practice: Look at a map, or picture one: China, the long land road running east, the peninsula reaching down toward Japan.
Trace the way a monk might have walked with a bundle of scriptures, over mountains and rivers, then close your eyes and sit with that slow road.

wordCard.voice: Korea. The peninsula where, the old histories record, a monk named Sundo arrived with images and scriptures, and the teaching took root kingdom by kingdom.

carryVoice: Your line: the teaching arrives. It came in a monk's bag and took its time. Day nine hundred nineteen, done.
